newsitem.title: LATVIA: FOCUS-LATVIAN DEFICIT NOT SEEN HITTING T-BILL YIELDS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-LATVIAN DEFICIT NOT SEEN HITTING T-BILL YIELDS.

text.p: The doubt which has been cast on Latvia's plan for a balanced budget was not seen having a significant impact on the country's domestic debt market, dealers said on Thursday.

Finance Minister Robert Ziles said on Thursday that the country's goal of a balanced budget was in jeoprady as income tax revenues would probably fall short of target and expenditure pressures were building up.
But Zile cautioned that the deficit would only reach the modest level of around ten million lats or 0.4 percent of GDP - well within the state's limits.
"If there is a deficit, it won't have much affect on T-bill rates, unless the government brings more paper to the market to fill the shortfall," said one local debt dealer.
"But the government has other instruments at its disposal," the dealer added.
Average yields on one and three-month T-bills fell at Wednesday's auction to 3.84 percent and 4.05 percent.
Some dealers said they are set to rise again but that the possibility of a budget deficit had little to do with the upward trend they see on the horizon.
"It (the decifit) won't have a big impact on the primary market," said Maris Vinklers, head of money markets at Hansabank-Latvija.
"The amount cited by the finance minister is too small," he said.
"T-bill rates will probably go up anyway, but for other reasons...demand for longer maturities is increasing and that will soon cut demand for shorter maturities," he said.

"Demand will also fall because new debt instruments, such as commericial papers and corporate bonds denominated in lats, are coming to the market. All of these factors should push T-bill yields up," he said.
A balanced budget was widely regarded as one of the crowning achievements of outgoing Prime Minister Andris Shkele's period at the helm of Latvia's government.

Shkele, who quit on Monday after he fell out with the governing parties, is a no-nonsense businessman credited with successfully pushing tough austerity measures through the fractious 100-seat parliament.
